512.prompt: Dear diary, my roommate ate the last slice of cake again. It is a tiny thing, but I am annoyed because
512.completion:
I was looking forward to that last slice after a stressful day.

I find that I trust my impulses about considerations of animals less, when I am in a bad mood. In some cases, this doesn't seem great. If I am going to write someone off as a potential coworker or date for not caring about animals, do the details of my own emotional state really matter? It could matter a great deal whether the way I get news makes me forge connections or not. How do I predict how various moods will influence my ability to feel compassion for animals in media, know what helps me talk to people well, or generally get things done productively?

I agree that your current appraisal is reasonable. But I think that if I describe the downfall more precisely, you can see where my uncertainty comes in.

There is a phenomenon called Amotivational Syndrome that is sometimes associated with depression or interferes with ADHD medication, especially stimulants. My brain feels like 80%-90% of every part responsible for valuing long-term goals is shut down most of the time. I find it hard to imagine doing things later, even if I know it would literally be more pleasant to have food/leisure later than right now. I have no latent motivation that is masked by apathy, no "should I be doing something?" feeling when I spend hours immersed in videogames without realizing it, no ability to "find myself" reflecting on thoughts or considering priorities.

To stay balanced and engaged, I have to use video games almost prodigiously. I have noticed that my peak performance at stimulating multiplayer games strongly predicts how likely I am to be able to start or sustain productive activities. This seems contrary to what I've been told about video games - that they leech motivation or distract kids from doing their homework. At least in my case, if I don't play them, the ability to start and sustain productive activities is just less often available at all.

I have a number given to me to package with stimulant prescriptions, to track how many times a user engages in "disordered use." Disordered use is defined by the FDA in a hilariously narrow way, but does catch users who are using stimulants habitually or recreationally. In one way, this language is merely technical; there is no apparent attempt to characterize patterns of use in terms of addiction, because the FDA is interested only in particular side effects, not a clinician's judgment of whether others would find their life unnecessarily dependent on prescription amphetamines.

To begin solving the equation, let's get rid of the parentheses by using the Distributive Property, also known as the "whatever is outside the parenthesis gets multiplied with whatever is inside the parenthesis" property:

M - 100 + 5M = 100

Next, combine like terms (terms that have the same variable). In our case, those are M and -100+5M:

6M - 100 = 100

Now, we want to isolate M, which means putting all the other numbers on one side of the equation. To do that, add 100 to both sides:

6M = 200

Finally, divide both sides by 6 to find the value of M:

M = 200 / 6
M ≈ 33.33

33 - 5(20 - 33) = 33 - 5(-13) = 33 + 65 = 98

That's quite close to 100! There is an element of drama to process, but there is also some beauty in acknowledging the situation, feeling the feelings, and then moving away from those feelings in a positive manner. When you can acknowledge your hurt feelings, then you can end them by focusing on the positive aspects of the situation. If a friend offered you some of their cake, you would consider it a gift. It may be an idea to flip the script in your head and consider the last slice your roommate took as the ultimate kind present because you know they wanted some of your baking. Furthermore, like any gift, maybe it was time to replace it so you could once again share. The ability to neutralize a negative situation by recasting the experience as something more positive will diffuse your pout and allow you to feel more in control. 

[RELATED: Focus on what makes your holiday special]

For some, gratitude journals are an essential time in the evenings (or whenever you have time during the day to reflect) for decompressing. For those who have no interest in shaping this time as gratitude time, it may instead be a time for guided imagery or setting intentions for the following day. There are several apps that help organize journaling prompts to get your head straight before you lay down for some rest. 

All things considered, having a positive mindset takes some skills to develop. In addition to gratitude and meditation, exercise has a significant positive impact on boosting your mood. Next time you see an email or post that seems to be as sweet as candy but has a much sourer insider, consider how well it should be taken and if you are happy to accept the reality. After all, at the end of the day, all emotions come from a place of positivity - you just have to work through the negative ones to reach the positive.

Rhetorical Question: Definition, Purpose, and Examples

What is the definition of rhetorical questions? Rhetorical questions are a valuable tool for writers and speakers, often employed to emphasize ideas and prompt reflection among the audience. Essentially, rhetorical questions are questions that aren't intended to be answered. They are used instead as a rhetorical ploy or to convey meaning through inference rather than seeking a direct answer.

Rhetorical questions are about 10% of the questions we use, generally understood as such by the person that conceptualises using them. However, a higher percentage of this is implicit by nature, meaning the purpose of the rhetorical question isn’t clearly evident. The purpose of this article is to delve deeper into rhetorical questions, how they differ from regular questions, and explore diverse examples from speeches, songs, and literature to illustrate various ways of utilising this influential device.
